articles.standfirst: Lista apresentada no Festival Interlagos reúne modelos de BMW, Leapmotor, Jaecoo, DFM, IM e GAC, com diferentes níveis de eletrificação. Há opções que chegam ainda em 2026.
articles.summary: Lista apresentada no Festival Interlagos reúne modelos de BMW, Leapmotor, Jaecoo, DFM, IM e GAC, com diferentes níveis de eletrificação. Há opções que chegam ainda em 2026.
articles.body:
Nesta semana, o g1 esteve no Festival Interlagos, no Autódromo de Interlagos, em São Paulo (SP), para mostrar as principais novidades anunciadas para o mercado automotivo. E não há como escapar de uma lista de SUVs.

Confira a seguir seis destaques, com informações técnicas e, em alguns casos, preço já confirmado:

O SUV totalmente elétrico inaugura a nova linguagem visual da marca alemã, com linhas mais quadradas e um toque de retrofuturismo dos anos 1980. No Brasil, já está disponível em versão única por R$ 582.950.

O principal destaque é a autonomia proporcionada pela bateria de 108,7 kWh: são 570 km com uma única carga . No modo de máxima economia, a marca promete alcance de até 800 km , suficiente para percorrer os cerca de 600 km entre São Paulo (SP) e Belo Horizonte (MG).

No interior, chama a atenção uma tela que atravessa o painel de ponta a ponta, posicionada próxima à base do para-brisa. O efeito visual lembra um holograma, embora não seja um.

O B10 REEV tem uma proposta mais simples que a do iX3. O SUV chega em setembro e ainda não tem preço divulgado.

O utilitário tem o mesmo visual do Leapmotor B10 já lançado no Brasil, que é totalmente elétrico e custa entre R$ 164.390 e R$ 182.990. O desenho traz poucos ângulos retos e um interior minimalista: até o ajuste dos retrovisores é feito pela central multimídia.

Nesta versão, o motor 1.5 aspirado a gasolina serve apenas para gerar energia. Quem movimenta as rodas é o motor elétrico, alimentado pela bateria.

A Leapmotor promete até 900 km de autonomia com o tanque cheio e a bateria totalmente carregada. A distância equivale a cerca de 90% dos 1.000 km que separam São Paulo (SP) de Brasília (DF).

Com uma proposta mais simples que a dos demais, o Jaecoo 5 também chega ao Brasil em setembro e ainda não teve o preço divulgado. Entre os modelos da lista, é o que tem o sistema de eletrificação mais simples: um híbrido pleno.

Nesse tipo de híbrido, a bateria é menor e não precisa ser ligada à tomada ou a um eletroposto. Ela é recarregada automaticamente pelo próprio funcionamento do carro, inclusive durante as frenagens.

É o mesmo tipo de sistema híbrido usado no Toyota Corolla Cross, por exemplo. Apesar do porte semelhante, o Jaecoo 5 tem quase o dobro da potência. O Jaecoo 5 entrega 224 cv , contra 122 cv do Corolla Cross híbrido.

A DFM é uma marca inédita no Brasil, e os primeiros carros chegam entre outubro e novembro. O Vigo é um dos dois modelos de estreia. O SUV elétrico tem proposta mais discreta e chega ao Brasil a partir de outubro, ainda sem preço divulgado.

O Vigo tem porte semelhante ao do BYD Yuan Pro e ao do GWM Ora 5. Entre os modelos a combustão, pode ser comparado ao Hyundai Creta. Suas linhas mais retas também lembram o visual do SUV coreano.

O interior é mais minimalista que o de outros carros chineses. Um exemplo é o painel de instrumentos digital, "escondido" entre dois vincos do painel.

Entre os modelos mais luxuosos da lista, o IM6 marca a estreia da divisão de luxo IM no Brasil. O SUV elétrico de estilo cupê chega ao país no fim de 2026 e terá até 767 cv de potência e 81,7 kgfm de torque .

Para efeito de comparação, a potência supera os 541 cv do Porsche 911 GTS .

O painel reúne duas telas digitais, uma de 26,3 polegadas e outra de 10,5 polegadas. O interior também tem sistema de som e bancos que lembram poltronas.

A marca não divulgou o preço, mas o g1 apurou que o modelo custará cerca de R$ 400 mil, aproximadamente um terço do valor cobrado pelo Porsche 911 GTS, que parte de R$ 1,2 milhão.

Este é o maior e mais caro carro já lançado pela GAC no Brasil. O preço é de R$ 399.990 , e o modelo já está disponível nas concessionárias da marca.

Um dos destaques é a bateria de 44,5 kWh do sistema híbrido plug-in. A capacidade supera a do carro elétrico mais vendido do país, o BYD Dolphin Mini, que tem até 38,8 kWh.

Segundo o Inmetro, o GS9 pode rodar até 114 km apenas no modo elétrico. A autonomia é suficiente para percorrer os cerca de 95 km entre São Paulo (SP) e Campinas (SP).

O SUV acomoda seis pessoas, tem acabamento em couro nappa e oferece ventilação, aquecimento e até massagem nos bancos da primeira e da segunda fileiras. Os assentos também podem ser reclinados, em uma configuração que lembra a primeira classe de aviões.

articles.title: Jota Quest se equilibra bem no balanço de Tim Maia em álbum com groove, energia boa, reverência, raridades e hits | G1
articles.body:
Capa do álbum 'Jota Quest & Tim Maia – Dance enquanto é tempo' — Foto: Divulgação

Título: Jota Quest & Tim Maia – Dance enquanto é tempo

♬ Nos aplicativos de áudio desde a noite de quinta-feira, 27 de agosto, o álbum “Jota Quest & Tim Maia – Dance enquanto é tempo” é um disco em que o grupo mineiro de soul pop canta o repertório do cantor carioca com o próprio Tim Maia.

Voz fundamental na construção do universo do funk e soul brasileiros, em movimento feito entre o fim da década de 1960 e o início dos anos 1960, Sebastião Rodrigues Maia (28 de setembro de 1942 – 15 de março de 1998) pavimentou caminho seguido pelo Jota Quest há 30 anos.

Sintomaticamente, o ponto de partida da trilha de sucesso da banda de Rogério Flausino (voz), Marco Túlio Lara (guitarra), Marcio Buzelin (teclados), PJ (baixo) e Paulinho Fonseca (bateria) foi o lançamento da segunda versão do álbum “J. Quest” (1996), editada em 1996 com regravação de funk de autoria de Tim e Paulo Ricardo, “Dance enquanto o tempo” (1976), lançada 20 anos antes por Tim.

Três décadas depois daquele disco de 1996, a música “Dance enquanto o tempo” reaparece no título – mas não no repertório – do álbum lançado pelo Jota Quest neste ano de 2026, lembrando o vínculo do quinteto com Tim Maia. Neste álbum de 2026, valorizado pela azeitada produção musical de PJ, baixista da banda, o Jota Quest se escora em Tim Maia.

Em maior ou menor grau, a voz do cantor é ouvida em dez das 16 músicas do álbum, o que justifica o nome de Tim Maia aparecer no título. A rigor, trata-se quase de um trabalho conjunto, que une postumamente a banda com o ator com o aval do filho de Tim, Carmelo Maia, creditado como coprodutor.

Como o primeiro single do álbum sinalizou em 4 de dezembro do ano passado, há quase nove meses, ao apresentar a gravação do funk-disco “Acenda o farol” (1978) o Jota Quest canta Tim Maia – com ou sem o cantor – com extrema reverência, várias vezes na fronteira do cover, como comprova a abordagem da balada “Você” (1969).

Ainda assim, seria injusto negar os méritos de álbum calcado na exuberância do groove dessa banda formada por grandes instrumentistas, músicos cujo virtuosismo que salta aos ouvidos com a mixagem de João Milliet e a masterização de Chris Gehringer, ambas primorosas.

Seja mergulhando com a rapper Negri Li na vibe festiva de “O descobridor dos sete mares” (Michel e Gilson Mendonça, 1983), seja caindo com o próprio Tim Maia no samba-soul “Gostava tanto de você” (Edson Trindade, 1973), o Jota Quest se equilibra bem no balanço do Síndico .

O groove aliciante da intro “Seroma” (2026) – tema inédito composto pela banda com base sobre a qual ouve-se a voz de Tim salpicar informações de caráter biográfico – dá a pista certeira do suingue do álbum.

A energia de “Jota Quest & Tim Maia – Dance enquanto é tempo” é boa. E os convidados ajudam a dar frescor a músicas mais ou menos batidas, caso de “Imunização Racional (Que beleza)” (1975), hit da controvertida fase Racional de Tim Maia, revivido pelo Jota Quest com o jovial trio Os Garotin e com Carlinhos Brown (na percussão). O molho de Thiaguinho também dá outro tempero ao samba-soul “Réu confesso” (1973), ainda que o balanço evoque o arranjo original da gravação original de Tim.

É justo reconhecer que o Jota Quest soube ir além dos greatest hits de Tim Maia na seleção do repertório, ainda que não tenha evitado sucessos óbvios como “Azul da cor do mar” (sofrido baladão soul de 1970 que ganhou outra tonalidade no arranjo contemporâneo do Jota), “Primavera” (Cassiano e Silvio Roachel, 1970) – faixa, aliás, com jeito de cover – e “Não quero dinheiro (Só quero amar)” (1971), outro cover, mas infalível em qualquer pista (fala de Tim é ouvida na introdução da faixa, mas quem canta é somente o vocalista Rogério Flausino).

Sem falar em “Vale tudo” (1983), funk também irresistível, revisitado pelo Jota Quest em feat com Tim Maia e com atualizações na letra politicamente incorreta (“Agora vale tudo”, sublinha Flausino).

Música composta por Tim em tributo a Minas Gerais, estado natal do Jota Quest, o funk “Vou com gás”(1979) – ouvido em feat virtual de Tim com Rogério Flausino – é grata surpresa do álbum “Jota Quest & Tim Maia – Dance enquanto é tempo”.

Outra bem-vinda raridade é “Estrela do meu show”, versão em português – escrita pelo próprio Tim – de “You're a the star of my show” (Allen Jones, Bertram Brown, Terry Bartlett, William Sumlin e Vince Ricari Williams), música do repertório da banda norte-americana de soul e R&B Kwick. Tim lançou “Você é a estrela do meu show” – com o você no título, pronome suprimido pelo Jota – em single obscuro de 1981. “Estrela do meu show” brilha muito no toque do Jota Quest.

Samba-soul de Tim em parceria com Hyldon, “I don’t know what to do with myself” (1971) tenta harmonizar o canto de Flausino com a voz suave de Mãeana, convidada surpreendente, enquanto a lembrança de “Sossego” (1978) traz Tony Tornado – um dos arquitetos do funk brasileiro – em gravação feita com a adesão de Lincoln Tornado, filho de Tony. “Sossego” é o maior sucesso do álbum de 1978 em que Tim Maia, atento aos sinais, inseriu o funk no universo da disco music , então dominante no universo pop.

Encerrado com o funk “Racional culture” (Beto Cajueiro, 1976), faixa na qual o Jota Quest rebobina versos falados por Tim Maia na gravação do álbum “Tim Maia Racional vol. 2” (1976), o álbum “Jota Quest & Tim Maia – Dance enquanto é tempo” oferece munição para detratores do quinteto em uma ou outra faixa. Até porque ninguém canta Tim Maia como Tim Maia. Contudo, o saldo é positivo porque o groove da banda anima o baile do início ao fim. A festa é boa!

A banda Jota Quest assina com Tim Maia (1942 – 1998) o álbum em que apresenta o inédito tema autoral 'Seroma' entre 15 músicas do repertório do cantor — Foto: Fernando Young / Divulgação

articles.title: Inside Ishaan Khatter’s 3-bedroom sea-facing Bandra home with vintage Bollywood film posters, sunset views, music and personal memorabilia
articles.summary: Ishaan Khatter’s Mumbai home is less about conventional luxury and more about creating a space that reflects his personality. The actor’s three-bedroo.
articles.body: Ishaan Khatter’s Mumbai home is less about conventional luxury and more about creating a space that reflects his personality. The actor’s three-bedroom apartment overlooking the Bandra seaface has been designed as a relaxed, artistic retreat where vintage cinema references, music, greenery and personal keepsakes come together.Designed by Sarah Sham of Essajees Atelier, the residence was transformed in just two-and-a-half months. Ishaan wanted the interiors to feel young, dynamic and inspiring rather than formal, resulting in a home where every room has its own visual identity, as reported by Architectural Digest in 2024.Ishaan Khatter’s Bandra home was designed as an artist’s retreatFor Ishaan, the ideal home was one where he could unwind after long days of filming and travelling. His love for quiet evenings spent watching the sunset with coffee and music became an important part of the design brief. The actor wanted an abode that felt lived-in rather than overly polished. Sarah Sham therefore brought together mix-and-match furniture, plants, varied textures and distinctive accents to create a laid-back yet characterful aesthetic. The project came together under an exceptionally tight timeline, with the entire apartment being overhauled in just 2.5 months.Eclectic interiors with vintage Bollywood references at Ishaan Khatter's homeThe apartment moves away from a uniform design language, with each room offering something different. Textured and mottled walls provide a layered backdrop, while vintage-inspired details add a sense of nostalgia. One wall features an excerpt from Rudyard Kipling’s poem If, while a corridor decorated with old Bollywood posters evokes the atmosphere of a classic film studio. These cinematic touches make the home particularly personal for an actor whose own career is rooted in Hindi cinema. The eclectic approach extends to the furniture as well, with the interiors deliberately avoiding a formal or overly coordinated appearance.Ishaan Khatter’s home theatre is his favourite spaceAmong the various rooms, the home theatre holds a special place for Ishaan. The room features a wall unit that serves multiple purposes, functioning as both a library and a display area for his scripts and trophies. For the actor, the space brings together two important aspects of his life — cinema and his personal collection of memories from his career. His guitar and cajon also find a place in the home, reflecting his interest in music and adding another creative dimension to the residence.Eclectic details add personality to Ishaan Khatter's homeThe apartment is filled with unexpected details that reflect Ishaan’s interests. A climber’s hangboard takes up a section of one bedroom wall, while the foyer features a lake-shaped mirror that brings a playful element to the interiors. These details reinforce the idea behind the home — it was never meant to look like a showroom. Instead, the design incorporates objects and references that feel connected to Ishaan's lifestyle.The living room reflects Ishaan’s idea of the perfect homeIshaan has described the living room as exactly the atmosphere he had envisioned for his home. The space combines comfortable furniture, plants and tactile surfaces to create a relaxed setting. The studio-cum-training room, meanwhile, was designed with functionality in mind, allowing the actor to work out and prepare for his projects without compromising on the overall aesthetic. The combination of practicality and individuality runs throughout the apartment, with each room serving a different purpose.A home inspired by sunsets, music and slow momentsDespite the apartment’s striking design elements, its overall mood remains intimate and relaxed. Ishaan’s routine of taking bike rides on Sunday mornings and spending evenings listening to music over coffee helped shape the feeling he wanted from the residence. The Bandra location adds another layer to that experience, with the sea-facing setting allowing the actor to enjoy sunsets from home. The result is a residence that balances youthful energy with nostalgia, from old Hindi film posters and scripts to musical instruments, books and personal memorabilia.More about Ishaan Khatter's work frontIshaan has had a particularly strong run of late, with acclaimed performances in 'Homebound' and 'The Royals' adding to his growing reputation as one of Bollywood's most versatile young actors. He recently served on the jury at the 2026 Biarritz Film Festival – Nouvelles Vagues in France alongside Kristen Stewart, a first for him on the international festival circuit. On the film front, he's gearing up for the release of 'Jugaadu', a comic entertainer produced under Baweja Studios and Tips Films, alongside an ensemble cast including Abhishek Banerjee and Jameel Khan. He is also preparing to start filming the second season of Netflix’s 'The Royals', scheduled to begin production this September. articles.body: Nayanthara and Kavin's 'Hi' has opened its theatrical run with an estimated Rs 1.23 crore net collection in India. The movie arrived in cinemas on Friday. The movie registered 33% overall occupancy across 786 shows.The Tamil version accounted for the majority of the reported earnings. It collected Rs 1.14 crore net on Day 1. The Telugu version contributed Rs 9 lakhs. With its opening-day performance, 'Hi' has now begun its box office journey.'Hi' language-wise collectionThe Tamil version emerged as the primary contributor to the movie's domestic earnings. Its Day 1 net collection stood at Rs 1.14 crore.The Telugu version recorded Rs 9 lakhs net. Together, the two versions took the India net collection to Rs 1.23 crore.The overall occupancy across the movie's reported shows stood at 33%. The film was screened across 786 shows on its opening day.'Hi' worldwide box office collectionThe movie's reported India gross collection currently stands at Rs 1.38 crore. After accounting for the reported domestic net earnings, the India net total is Rs 1.23 crore. The worldwide gross collection is currently reported at Rs 1.38 crore.What is 'Hi' about?'Hi' follows Mayilsamy, played by Kavin, whose repeated experiences with romantic rejection have left him struggling to find a relationship. His circumstances change after he encounters Devayani, played by Nayanthara.Devayani is trying to avoid an arranged marriage. Her father Indhiran, played by Prabhu, has accepted Rs 57 lakh from the family of her prospective groom. articles.title: Reading Festival goer says solo experience is 'a lot nicer'
articles.summary: Solo festivalgoer Tilly Davies talks about feeling safe, making friends and having "a great time".
articles.body:
It is the second time Tilly Davies is attending Reading Festival by herself.

The 18-year-old, from Northamptonshire, said even though it could get "a bit lonely", it was possible to make friends and, once you get to enjoy the music, "it doesn't really affect you much".

Last year, she was supposed to come to the annual event with friends but they could not get tickets.

Despite that, Tilly has once again made it to Richfield Avenue on her own, ready for the weekend ahead, and says she is having "such a great time" and would definitely recommend the solo experience to others. "It's a lot nicer going alone," she said, adding it meant she could go and see whichever act she liked.

The event is expected to welcome about 100,000 people this year , with headliners such as Charli XCX.

Tilly is most excited for Sunday, when Florence and the Machine and Chase & Status will take to the stage.

"Just get out of your comfort zone, it's not as scary as you think," she said when asked about her solo visit.

"It's scary getting there by yourself at first but, once you're there, it's so easy to make friends and you're going to have a great time."

She said a few people were "surprised" at her decision but she had enjoyed last year.

"My friends couldn't get tickets last year, and I just had such a great time, being able to just go and watch whoever I wanted and not have to think about who everyone else wanted to go and watch, so I thought I'd do it again."

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

She said it was going well for her so far this year and the only obstacle had been carrying her equipment alone.

"It was very heavy. I seem to have brought more than I did last year, so it was a bit of a struggle, but it was alright."

Tilly said she felt safe and security were "great".

"You can go and find someone who works here and, if you have any issues, they'll sort it out straight away."

She said anyone worried about safety issues should "definitely stay in one of the separate campsites".

"It makes you feel a lot safer knowing that people can't just go into the campsite without a ticket for it."

Tilly said people who got "a bit confused" on why she was going alone "just haven't experienced it alone".

"It's a lot nicer going alone but it is also nice having friends, so it's good to go out and make friends with people when you're there," she said.

"It can be quite lonely mainly if you're at your tent.

"But, when you're going and watching the music, you're there having a great time, so it doesn't really affect you much."

articles.title: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
articles.summary: Police say at least six other people were also injured in the incident at the Big Church Festival.
articles.body:
Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a sign fell at their event and injured seven people, with one man dying at the scene.

Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park , near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.

It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.

The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.

Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them.

"And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.

"May the god of comfort and healing be with them all."

South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.

The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.

The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.

"We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said.

"We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

The Reverend James Di Castiglione, rector of the parish of Chanctonbury in which Big Church Festival takes place, says the incident has been a "huge shock to everyone locally".

"We are all experiencing emotional whiplash about what's happened really because Big Church Festival is such a time of joy and unity and love and celebration," he added.

Di Castiglione said at the event there was "just a sense of confusion and shock that was rippling across the site".

"[It is] just the worst lightning bolt of tragic news striking everybody's hearts," he said.

The Salvation Army in Hove had opened its hall on Friday to allow people to stay the night if they could not get home after the event was cancelled.

Martin Bellshaw, from the Hove branch, said they welcomed about 20 people from Bristol and the north-west of England.

Christian parent support charity ParentFuel said its people at the festival were all safe.

"We cannot praise the BCF (Big Church Festival) team enough for the way things have been handled," they said on social media on Saturday morning.

"We are currently sat in the volunteer tent with a brew in hand, worship music being played and the warmth of chatter around us."

The charity said it was a "freak accident".

"Life is so precious and so, so short. This weekend brought that ever closer for us all," they added.

Theo Saville, who was at the festival, said a "large wooden sign" had collapsed near the entrance to a tented area.

Sussex Police is urging anyone with information about the incident to contact them.

The Health and Safety Executive and local authority had also been informed, the force added.

articles.title: How Massive Attack's legacy is changing major UK festivals
articles.summary: For the first time, all of Forwards Festival's stages will be powered by green energy.
articles.body:
When Massive Attack set the world record for producing the lowest ever carbon emissions at a gig, the duo hoped it would create a ripple effect across the industry.

And this weekend, as 60,000 descend on Bristol for Forwards Festival, their dream is being realised. For the first time in the music event's history, every stage will be powered by renewable energy.

Other major events including Love Saves the Day and Bristol International Balloon Fiesta also swapped diesel generators for green technology this year.

Massive Attack's Robert Del Naja said their 2024 show was always about systemic change, adding it was gratifying to see this permanent legacy of decarbonisation for festivals.

The 2024 ACT 1.5 Massive Attack music festival in Bristol produced 98% less power-related emissions than comparable shows by being 100% battery powered and selling 100% vegan food, among other things.

Following a record-breaking summer of prolonged heat and dry weather, which has been influenced by human-induced climate change , the duo are hoping more events will introduce sustainable options.

The changes have been made possible with funding from a Clean Power Pilot led by the West of England Combined Authority (Weca), running this summer.

Helen Godwin, Weca mayor, said: "After another exceptionally hot and dry summer, everyone can see how our climate is changing.

"Here in the West of England, we've brought together our brilliant creative industries and clean energy sectors to try to help tackle the climate crisis and clean up our air."

"We've always been a region that cares about our environment, cares about clean energy, about clean air. But we also love to have a good time," said Godwin.

She added that producing dirty air affects people's health.

articles.title: Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
articles.summary: The spread of AI-generated EDM music is creating a culture of callouts and mistrust among artists.
articles.body: As audio-focused generative tools and platforms have gotten more sophisticated, the internet has become increasingly filled with AI-generated music whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content immediately own up to using AI, others have denied using the technology until increasing public scrutiny forced them to tell the truth. For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is “real” and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex; listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art. [Media: When I recently spoke with Harris, he told me that he sees AI-generated music as “a kind of decoy art form,” and he thinks that the people making it don’t really have anything meaningful to say with their creations. He feels that true art in any medium is “created by people that are trying to express feelings and messages,” and he believes that the only thing AI boosters are really interested in is making a quick profit. “I don’t consider AI-generated material to be art, and I don’t think this technology is really advancing art in any meaningful way,” Harris said. “It’s a technological advancement that’s giving people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.” Harris, originally from Maine, described his approach to making music as being fairly similar to working in other creative mediums. He always begins with a core concept before he starts “throwing more ideas down until I find something that sticks.” And as complicated as his workflow might look to someone unfamiliar with all of the tools and programs that he uses — his production setup includes Ableton Live, Novation Launchkey 49 MIDI controller, Ableton Push 3, Launchpad X, a couple of analog synthesizers, Serum, Diva, and the software sampler Kontakt — he said that the entire process is “really just me making creative decisions” that culminates in a sound that feels right. “Each of those decisions — and there’s hundreds of them to go into each song — brings me closer to evoking a specific kind of idea or emotion,” Harris explained. “And then once I have a song mapped out, I have to start making even more choices about how to mix it in a way that makes it sound good and presentable.” In Harris’ view, being a real artist means being able to make those kinds of experimental but informed creative decisions using your own studied understanding of a given medium. One of Harris’ biggest issues with gen AI is the way the technology often eliminates a user’s need to think about how songs (or books, films, podcasts, etc.) come together. But he has also been dismayed at the way that AI posers are muddying listeners’ understanding of what human-made EDM actually sounds like. “Aside from the similar vocals, you can usually hear a sharp hissing throughout the track,” Harris said of AI-generated songs. “I think that comes from the way that these models often work by starting with a big white noise block and then making guesses about waveforms by referencing data taken from real songs.” Harris pointed to MANSA’s “Midnight on My Mind” and Danny and Ian Asher’s “Take Me (To The Moon)” as what he thinks are examples of AI-produced songs that embody what he jokingly refers to as “the AI revolution” that’s responsible for polluting the EDM space. MANSA, Danny, and Asher have not publicly commented on whether they use generative tools in their music. But Harris and other EDM fans have noticed the similarities between “Take Me (To The Moon)” and another person’s AI-generated track. There’s no definitive evidence that MANSA produced “Midnight on My Mind” with AI. Harris could very well be wrong about these songs being generated with AI. But his insistence that they are reflects the larger culture of mistrust that has developed in response to the growing presence of AI content online. Harris holds AI production company Suno responsible for the recent spike in this kind of music being uploaded to the internet, but he also credits specific quirks of the platform for helping him learn how to spot songs worth calling out. “Something I’ve noticed with a lot of Suno-generated tracks is that a lot of the time, you’ll hear the vocals and other melodic elements will start stuttering at the same exact time,” Harris explained. “These models still have a hard time fully separating different parts of the songs they’re trained on, and they treat these elements like one big instrument. As a music producer, all of these things come across like choices that a human just wouldn’t make with their compositions because it just doesn’t make sense.” In some instances, the visuals accompanying AI tracks are part of what prompts Harris to accuse people of slinging AI. You might not be able to hear the generative models behind evangelical Christian AI persona Lionsaddle’s music, but you can clearly see the character’s fingers vanishing in and out of existence in videos. There is also an overly glossy visual quality to most of the videos posted by Christian house musician Midnite Manna that makes their content look a lot like what we typically refer to as AI slop. [Media: Suno also came up multiple times during my conversation with 39-year-old Italian turntabilist-turned-producer Nihil Young. Young’s posts on Threads about people using Suno are what initially inspired Harris to make his videos. Like Harris, Young has spent the past few months watching multiple EDM newcomers’ stars rise after they post music he thinks was generated with AI tools like Suno’s. And while Young isn’t usually one to get involved with online discourse, he felt it was important to speak out about how many people are flooding the scene with AI tracks. “These songs are the sound of Suno, which to me means that the people behind the songs are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking the platform to remix them,” Young told me, referring to Josh Fawaz’s “Like a Prayer” cover, which now includes AI credits following a wave of online backlash. “If they can do it with major artists like her, they can do it with you, me, and everyone else, which just isn’t cool. They can take your entire catalog, feed it to Suno, and generate ‘new’ songs from that stolen work.” Young claimed that in response to his Threads posts, he received multiple hacking attempts and a wave of online harassment from AI defenders. He also told me that he thinks people bought fake followers to boost his Spotify numbers as a way of casting doubt on his authenticity. That spooked Young — who is raising a young daughter and just put out a new album of his own — to rethink whether he should continue. He’s taken a break from callouts, but he still thinks it’s important to know about the way AI music is harming human artists. “Music production is where most of my income comes from, and almost as soon as AI began rolling out, I started losing many of my clients,” said Young, who has previously done audio mixing and mastering work for Sony Music, Warner, and Universal. “I can only imagine what it’s been like for singers, graphics artists, and people working in other creative fields. Whether you realize it or not, this stuff is impacting everyone.” What Young wishes more listeners could appreciate is how easy it has become to generate entire songs with platforms like Suno. In his opinion, most people using AI to make music “aren’t actually doing anything creative and they don’t have a true artistic process” because many generative tools on the market involve some degree of autogeneration. When I brought up how detailed AI prompts can be, he insisted that many of the people posting AI music likely aren’t even writing their own inputs. Young noted that Suno’s Simple Mode allows users to whip up songs by simply selecting a musical genre and clicking a button — a process that requires basically zero thinking. (Suno has not responded to a request for comment in time for publication.) As much as traditional artists might loathe generative production, there is no denying that AI songs are making their way into the mainstream. In 2024, Metro Boomin took shots at Drake with a beat sampling comedian King Willonius’ “BBL Drizzy” — an AI track whose vocals, melodies, and instrumental elements were generated by AI music startup Udio. Metro Boomin’s “BBL Drizzy” went viral after the producer posted the beat to SoundCloud and invited other performers to rap over it. Drake subsequently rapped over the beat himself on Sexyy Red’s “U My Everything,” and that song managed to peak at 44 on the Billboard Hot 100. Wholly AI-generated songs (and people) are finding success, as well. Last summer, Vinih Pray’s Suno-created song “A Million Colors” also peaked at 44 on TikTok’s Viral 50 chart, and AI artists Breaking Rust and Cain Walker made it onto Billboard’s Country Digital Song sales chart — a lesser-known chart focusing on individual song downloads. Meanwhile, Hallwood Media — a label founded by former Geffen Records president Neil Jacobson — signed AI avatar Xania Monet to a $3 million recording deal. Certain segments of the industry are clearly trying to normalize AI-generated music, and people are definitely making money with their machine-generated tracks. Kapwing estimates that the top 10 most followed / streamed AI music creators on Spotify and YouTube collectively raked in over $6 million in 2025. And with platforms like Deezer reporting that AI songs now account for over 50 percent of new uploads, that kind of music is getting harder for listeners to avoid — if they can even recognize it. While streaming platforms are beginning to more clearly label AI songs, many listeners have reported that they can’t really hear the difference between generative and human-made music. Aside from the people uploading all of these songs, no one has a way of being absolutely certain whether the tracks were generated with AI or made by an actual artist. AI music detection tools are one potential solution, but it’s not entirely clear how and, perhaps more importantly, if listeners might incorporate them into their lives. Judging by the numbers (which, of course, can be manipulated with paid streams), there do seem to be people who don’t mind the sounds of Suno and other AI tools. Young knows that most people’s ears probably aren’t well-attuned to identifying audio slop, but he still thinks that music lovers owe it to themselves to make the effort to find real, human artists. “In my opinion, it becomes obvious that you’re listening to AI-generated music when you put on a good pair of headphones,” Young told me. “But I also think that a lot of people these days are consuming music like fast food and listening to it through the speakers on their phone. Or they just have it on a background noise, and they don’t necessarily care what it sounds like.”

articles.title: Meghan Markle's acting U-turn exposes 'lingering problem' after six years of reinventions: experts
articles.summary: Meghan Markle remains in talks to join "The Gentlemen" Season 3, raising questions about six years of post-royal reinvention.
articles.body: Meghan Markle spent years trying to reinvent herself after leaving royal life — but her latest move could bring her right back to where she started. With Season 3 of "The Gentlemen" officially greenlit, the Duchess of Sussex remains in talks to join Guy Ritchie's hit drama, People magazine reported, contradicting earlier reports that the potential deal had fallen through. No deal has been finalized, the outlet said. "If she returns now, it raises the obvious question — what happened to all those other identities she tried on after leaving royal life?" Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. MEGHAN MARKLE’S ACTING RETURN COULD SPARK FRESH PROBLEMS WITH PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERT "Podcaster, producer, lifestyle entrepreneur, philanthropist, media mogul," said Schofield. "Returning to acting would suggest that the most viable professional identity Meghan has found may ultimately be the one she walked away from." The talks are in "very early stages," Deadline previously reported. It’s unclear how many episodes she would appear in. The series, which stars Theo James, Kaya Scodelario and Giancarlo Esposito, is filmed in the U.K. and set in England. Meghan has already dipped her toe back into acting. In 2025, she filmed a small cameo as herself in Amazon MGM Studios' upcoming comedy "Close Personal Friends," starring Brie Larson, Lily Collins, Jack Quaid and Henry Golding. The potential role in "The Gentlemen," however, would mark a more significant return to scripted acting after leaving "Suits." WATCH: MEGHAN MARKLE COULD REVIVE CAREER WITH SHOCKING ACTING RETURN: EXPERT "The Gentlemen" follows Eddie Horniman (Theo James), who unexpectedly inherits his father’s title as Duke of Halstead and the family’s sprawling estate after his father dies — only to discover that Halstead Manor sits atop a massive cannabis operation and that his reckless older brother has been passed over. Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, told Fox News Digital that Meghan's potential Hollywood comeback could expose the challenge that has followed her for years: finding an identity once the camera stops rolling that sticks. "This has been the lingering problem for Meghan all these years: what is her identity?" he said. "She's ridden a carousel of career horses. Yet for all the rotations, nothing has seemingly stuck." In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story." The spokesperson confirmed that the couple's business operations will remain based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their California home. People magazine reported that Meghan's potential acting project contributed to the couple's decision to return to Britain. Schofield isn't convinced that filmmakers will now embrace Meghan with open arms. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "I'm still skeptical that this represents some grand Hollywood comeback," she said. "Meghan has spent six years in [California] with a multimillion-dollar Netflix relationship, enormous name recognition and Tyler Perry on speed dial. If acting was genuinely her ambition, she was already standing in arguably the best place in the world to pursue it." "That said, 'The Gentlemen' would be a clever choice," she noted. "It's an established hit with a strong creative pedigree, so she wouldn't have to carry the project herself. But first, she has to prove she can disappear into a character rather than have every scene become about Meghan Markle." In 2022, when asked by Variety whether she would ever return to acting, Meghan replied: "I’m done." "I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not," she said at the time. Since stepping back from royal duties in 2020, Meghan has launched a series of ventures with mixed results. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Her high-profile Spotify partnership ended in 2023 after her podcast, "Archetypes," produced one season. Her planned Netflix animated series "Pearl" was scrapped before reaching production. Her lifestyle brand, originally launched as American Riviera Orchard, endured a prolonged rollout before being relaunched to As Ever in 2025. In March 2026, a Sussex spokesperson confirmed that her Netflix lifestyle series, "With Love, Meghan," would continue as seasonal specials rather than return for a third season. Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, told Fox News Digital that after years of reinvention, Meghan may have little to lose by returning to the career that first put her in the spotlight. "The honest picture is more complicated than any of the tabloid headlines and narratives about the empire," he explained. "'With Love, Meghan' became a punchline when it needed to be a launchpad. And when the show was mocked, it poisoned the well for As Ever as well, because the credibility was gone. The problem is that she and Harry believed the big Netflix deals and Spotify checks meant they had leverage when, actually, the checks were the leverage." "The most interesting path forward for Meghan, and several sources raised this unprompted to Celebrity Intelligence, is a return to acting would actually be a wise move," he continued. "Find an extraordinary script the way Demi Moore did with 'The Substance' and do something that shocks people. Get away from this princess arc and go back to what you loved and what made you famous in the first place." Meghan, daughter of Emmy-winning lighting director Thomas Markle, got her start in Hollywood with bit parts on shows like "Fringe" and "The League." She was also a suitcase model on "Deal or No Deal" before becoming a series regular as Rachel Zane in the legal drama "Suits." She filmed her final scenes in 2017 following her engagement, and her final episode aired in April 2018. PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "Of all the professional reinventions Meghan has attempted, acting makes the most sense," said Schofield. "She has legitimate experience doing it. She spent years working consistently on 'Suits.' There's nothing embarrassing about returning to the profession that originally made her successful." "What I find amusing is the contradiction," she said. "Meghan spent years presenting herself as though acting was something she had evolved beyond. Perhaps the great reinvention is discovering that the original brand worked better than all the rebrands." Stepping back in front of the camera could work in Meghan’s favor. Recent polls have placed both Harry and Meghan near the bottom of the royal family’s popularity rankings in Britain, ahead of only former Prince Andrew, People magazine reported. But if there's one thing Meghan has consistently proven, it's her ability to command attention — the enduring power of the so-called "Markle Sparkle." "Meghan brings something you cannot manufacture with a marketing budget, and that's global curiosity," said Schofield. "Love her or loathe her, people will watch the first episode just to see whether she can still act. Every photograph from the set becomes international news. Every trailer gets dissected. Every interview generates headlines." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "From a publicity standpoint, I completely understand why a producer might take that gamble," she said. "The question is whether the spectacle surrounding Meghan ultimately serves the story or overwhelms it. But there's an enormous difference between attracting attention and building a sustainable career. The real test is whether anybody wants to see Meghan's character again once the novelty wears off."

articles.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Dolly Parton taught the world the way to be universally beloved
articles.summary: Dolly Parton navigated tough interviews from Barbara Walters to political questions about Trump while building an ironclad legacy of kindness.
articles.body: When the news broke that Dolly Parton had died at age 80, the networks exploded in tributes and primetime specials about her career in music and acting and her plethora of good works. Everyone remarked on how rare it was that someone could be universally beloved. How could that be done? Some of the answer to that is simple: Be kind to everyone. Be generous in spirit and with your wealth. One crucial thing, especially in the last 10 years, is to steer entirely clear of politics, if such a thing is possible. The media has tried to shame entertainers who refuse to speak on politics. Dolly brought her aura of celebrity and philanthropy in a way that she could escape the shaming attempts. But she perfected the formula a long time ago, ingratiating herself to a broad audience. One of the old TV clips making the rounds was a 1977 interview on ABC with Barbara Walters, who asked questions that could come across as offensive, even hostile. "Dolly, where I come from, would I have called you a hillbilly?" She hinted that parts of her body might be artificial: "Is it all you?" DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY Then, about her appearance in general, Walters pressed: "You don't have to look like this. You're very beautiful. You don't have to wear the blonde wigs. You don't have to wear the extreme clothes, right? ... Do you ever feel that you're a joke that people make fun of you?" Dolly never took offense. Walters had a habit of trying to ask questions the audience at home might be thinking, so these questions were a chance to address them. Perhaps the roughest question was about how she didn’t see much of her husband Carl Dean on the road, so Walters asked if the love was real, and, "Why have a husband away someplace to see six weeks a year?" STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING Walters was married four times to three different men, so maybe she was reflecting on her own nature, if not Dolly’s, who was married to her husband for almost 60 years, until he died last year. In 2018, Dolly talked to ABC correspondent David Wright, and he brought up the plot of the movie "9 to 5" and then tried to relate that to President Donald Trump: "The sexist, egotistical, lying, hypocritical bigot portrayed so effectively in that movie by actor Dabney Coleman hasn’t exactly disappeared from the culture. We have a president of the United States who said the things on that bus." (That would be the audio that leaked in 2016 where Trump mused to "Access Hollywood" host Billy Bush about grabbing women.) Dolly rolled out her usual answer: "I'm not addressing that. I do not get into that. Of course, I have my opinion about everybody and everything. But I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business. I'm not in politics. I am an entertainer." The ABC correspondent whined, "And yet you’re also a role model." She replied: "Yes, I am. That's why I don't talk about people." After her passing, NBC touted that it had conducted over 50 interviews with Dolly on "Today," and noted that Robert Goldblatt, who helped Dolly create the Broadway musical version of "9 to 5," became the chairman of NBC Entertainment, and they partnered in two "Coat of Many Colors" movies about Dolly’s childhood, in 2015 and in 2016. DOLLY PARTON OFFERED TO TRY EXPERIMENTAL DRUGS IF ‘NO HOPE’ FOR CANCER BATTLE TO HELP OTHERS, SISTER SAYS It was her father’s inability to read and write that spurred Dolly to create her most celebrated charity, the Imagination Library, in 1995. They have distributed over 300 million books to children to promote literacy. That’s a good cause, no matter what your politics might be. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Her other philanthropic works, from funding disaster relief after local wildfires in Tennessee to development of the COVID-19 vaccine, built that ironclad positive reputation. But as you can tell from all of this week’s outpouring of testimony from famous and not-famous people about her kindness and supportive nature, she also built her reputation, day by day, in many interactions with people who were just astonished to be in her presence. To remain humble after all her fame and fortune defies the stereotype of self-obsessed celebrities. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP To people who have been granted so much, it’s a challenge to give back, and Dolly Parton seemed to return every demand on her attention with patience and grace. It’s no wonder everyone marvels at her example. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM TIM GRAHAM

articles.title: Dolly Parton's path from Nashville newcomer to Billboard's No. 1 country music artist of all time
articles.summary: Dolly Parton gained national attention in 1964 on "The Porter Wagoner Show," later becoming a 10-time Grammy Award-winner and Academy Award nominee.
articles.body: Dolly Parton's career as an entertainer spanned roughly seven decades. During that time, the legendary country music star cemented herself as an icon not only in the music industry, but also as a movie star and a philanthropist. From getting her start on "The Porter Wagoner Show" in 1964 to multiple Academy Award nominations, Parton forged a path for herself in the industry and paved the way for female country singers who followed her. DOLLY PARTON’S SIX-DECADE LOVE STORY WITH CARL DEAN BEGAN AT A LAUNDROMAT Here are some of Parton's career highlights. "The Porter Wagoner Show" Parton moved to Nashville, Tennessee, in May 1964, the day after graduating from high school, to pursue a career in country music. Three years later, she released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in February 1967, which caught the attention of singer Porter Wagoner. He then invited Parton to join him on his TV show, "The Porter Wagoner Show," a few months later, in September 1967. Parton's time on the show provided her with national attention and established her as a recording artist. Her duets with Wagoner, starting with "The Last Thing on My Mind," became major country hits. Their partnership also earned Parton her first Grammy nomination in 1970. In addition to her duets with Wagoner, she also released many of her well-known songs during this era, including "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "My Tennessee Mountain Home," "Just Because I'm a Woman" and many more. After seven years on the show, Parton felt it was time to pursue a solo career, ultimately leaving the show in 1974. Solo success Shortly after leaving the show, Parton released "Love Is Like a Butterfly," which quickly climbed to the top of the Billboard country charts. She continued releasing hit after hit, including "Here You Come Again," off the album with the same name, which earned her first Grammy Award win in 1979. She had 26 songs reach No. 1 on the Billboard country charts, including "The Bargain Store," "Heartbreaker," "Starting Over Again," "Tennessee Homesick Blues" and "Why'd You Come in Here Lookin' Like That." In addition to her own music, Parton found success covering other artists' songs in her own style, including "Stairway to Heaven," "The House of the Rising Sun," "Shine" and others. "Yes, and they loved it. Robert’s been out on tour, so he’s been doing a lot of interviews," she told Hot Press in 2002 about Led Zeppelin singer Robert Plant's reaction to her "Stairway to Heaven" cover. "And he seems to make mention of it a lot – I guess because people are asking him about it – and he says something different every time, but he seems to like it. He says he really likes what I did with it, and that makes me feel good." "I Will Always Love You" Parton wrote one of her most well-known songs, "I Will Always Love You," in 1973 when she told Wagoner she wanted to leave the show and go solo. When Wagoner responded negatively and all her efforts to get him to understand her reasoning fell on deaf ears, Parton thought she would put all her feelings into a song and play it for him to help him understand. "I said, ‘Porter, sit down. I got something I need to sing to you,’" she told Howard Stern in 2023. "He was just sitting behind his desk and tears started rolling down. He said, ‘That’s just the best song you ever wrote, and you can go if I can produce the song.’" The song was released in 1974 as part of her "Jolene" album, and climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart. It returned to No. 1 again in 1982 when Parton released a different version for "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." Nearly two decades after the song's initial release, Whitney Houston's version reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart, where it stayed for 14 consecutive weeks. Houston recorded an R&B ballad version of the song for the soundtrack to "The Bodyguard." In addition to staying at the No. 1 spot for 14 weeks, it was Billboard's No. 1 song of 1993, went 19-times Platinum in the U.S., and won two Grammy Awards at the 1994 ceremony. This version of the song is also the highest-selling single written by a female artist. "I almost wrecked, honest to god. I had to pull over to a Walgreens … and listen to the rest of it," Parton told Stern about hearing Houston's version for the first time. "I couldn’t believe my little country sad song could even be done like that … and it was just overwhelming. That was one of the greatest experiences I ever had in my entire life." "Dolly!" and "Dolly" variety shows Two years after leaving "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton started her own variety show called "Dolly!" in 1976. The show aired 26 half-hour episodes and featured guest stars such as Kenny Rogers, Linda Ronstadt, Emmylou Harris, Anne Murray and many others. Ten years after that show ended, she released a second variety show, "Dolly," in 1987. The show aired 22 one-hour episodes from September 1987 to May 1988 and was a huge ratings success, featuring guests such as Oprah Winfrey, Bruce Willis and Loretta Lynn as well as Kermit the Frog and Miss Piggy. Iconic collaborations In addition to Wagoner, Parton had several other significant collaborations throughout her career. One of her most celebrated partnerships was with Kenny Rogers. The two first connected in 1983 when they recorded the hit song, "Islands In the Stream" together. The song was a massive crossover hit and spent two consecutive weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and earned them a Grammy nomination. The two later released a joint Christmas album in 1984, titled "Once Upon a Christmas," and a year later collaborated on "Real Love," which reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot Country Singles chart. Nearly 30 years later, they released "You Can't Make Old Friends" in 2013, the title track of Rogers' album with the same name, earning them another Grammy nomination. "It really made me very emotional," Parton told ABC News in September 2013 about the song. "Even when I was recording it I was tearful, and when I was listening to the demo it really just, you know, it certainly summed us up and our relationship. But it also is such a song of friendship of all kinds." Parton also partnered with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt in 1987 to release their highly successful album, "Trio," which largely featured covers, except for "Wildflowers," which was written by Parton for the album. The album reached No. 1 on Billboard's country albums chart and No. 6 on the Billboard 200 and earned the three artists a Grammy. They followed it with "Trio II" in 1999, which featured a highly praised cover of Neil Young's song "After the Gold Rush," which earned them yet another Grammy. In addition to these collaborations, Parton released songs with Brad Paisley, Vince Gill, Willie Nelson, Reba McEntire, Miley Cyrus and others. Movie career After making a name for herself in the music world, she set her sights on movies. Parton made her feature film debut in the 1980 classic comedy "9 to 5," which also starred Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Tomlin, Fonda and Parton played a trio of secretaries who took revenge on their sexist boss by kidnapping him and enacting changes in the workplace in his name. The movie was an instant classic, earning Parton three Golden Globe nominations and an Oscar nomination for best original song for the song she wrote for the film, "9 to 5." Two years later, Parton made a splash with a second critically-acclaimed role in the film "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," playing Miss Mona, a madam at the Chicken Ranch, a long-running Texas brothel. Her role in the film earned her another Golden Globe nomination. She then starred in the 1989 movie "Steel Magnolias," alongside Hollywood heavy-hitters Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis and Julia Roberts. Together they portrayed a group of Southern women who banded together during life's good and hard moments, with Parton in particular playing a hair stylist. "I totally related to her. She's not different from me at all, and it wasn't hard for me to play a Southern girl with a Southern accent," she told "Today" in 1989. "And it's not foreign to me, like you said in your intro, for me to do hair, 'cause I grew up doing my sister's hair, my friends' hair – I started cutting and bleaching in a salon on my own at 15 years old and I loved it." Throughout her career, she also appeared in the films "Rhinestone," "Straight Talk," "The Beverly Hillbillies," "Miss Congeniality 2: Armed and Fabulous," "Joyful Noise" and others, including appearing on three episodes of "Hannah Montana." Award wins and nominations Parton received many accolades during her roughly seven decades in the entertainment industry. Since releasing her first album in 1967, Parton has received a total of 55 Grammy Award nominations, resulting in 10 wins. Her first win came in 1979 in the female country vocal performance for her song "Here You Come Again." articles.title: Stunned couple unearths 150-pound mystery hidden beneath their backyard for decades
articles.summary: A San Francisco couple unearthed a remarkable 150-pound limestone sculpture in their Russian Hill backyard, sparking a mystery with possible ties to artist Ralph Stackpole.
articles.body: A couple in San Francisco recently unearthed a 150-pound limestone sculpture buried in their backyard — setting off a search to uncover who created it and how it got there. Greg Gatwood was doing yard work at the couple's Russian Hill home in May when he came across what he initially thought was a piece of concrete buried in the ground as his partner Judy Gittelsohn stood nearby. Gatwood told Fox News Digital he tried to pry the object loose with a shovel before grabbing a pickaxe — and then spotted what appeared to be lips and a nose "peering" back at him. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY "I thought, well, maybe I should just break it into smaller pieces," Gatwood said. "Then I realized it was a statue. "It was like something you see in a movie, almost cinematic, you know — a big beautiful statue like this." Gittelsohn said she was stunned when Gatwood showed her the enormous, two-foot-wide statue — and was impressed by the quality of its craftsmanship. "I was just shocked," she said. "What an enormous find." ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ARTIFACT DEPICTING PHARAOH THOUGHT TO HAVE CHALLENGED MOSES IN EXODUS She added, "I was surprised. I was just gobsmacked." Three months after their discovery, the couple is still searching for answers. Gittelsohn, a professional artist, said she researched the sculpture. She believes it dates to the 1930s and may be connected to artists working under the Works Progress Administration (WPA). The couple's home is near the former San Francisco Art Institute, where prominent sculptor Ralph Stackpole taught for decades — leading Gittelsohn to believe the piece may have a connection to him or one of his students. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER One clue supporting that theory, she said, is that the sculpture was carved from relatively inexpensive limestone rather than costlier materials such as marble or granite. Gatwood believes the statue may have been used as garden art and that it was eventually buried with time. "It's quite possible this statue was displayed in the garden and not so much buried, but just lost," he said. After the couple received local attention for their find, Gittelsohn said a 93-year-old woman took an Uber to their home with her walker and knocked on their door. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The woman — one of several people who have reached out to the couple since the discovery became public — told them she had previously held a show featuring Ralph Stackpole's work. In September, the couple plans to put the sculpture on public display at the American Messenger Gallery in hopes that someone may recognize the piece or know who created it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "We think someone will eventually recognize it," Gatwood said. The story comes about a year after a New Orleans couple made a similarly mysterious discovery in their backyard. Sometimes, it happens right there in the bathroom. "I run every day… I found being a mom, if I can get 30 minutes of my cardio, it helps my mind... It gets me like sort of a little bit more regulated with my nervous system, so I really like that," she shared when asked about her go-to workout with a hectic schedule. HILARIA BALDWIN SHARES MARRIAGE LESSON SHE TELLS FRIENDS AFTER SURVIVING 'UPS AND OUR DOWNS' WITH ALEC BALDWIN "Then I obviously do my yoga, my little bathroom workouts, or just like a stop-and-drop little workout. Last month, she gave her fans a front-row look at exactly what those workouts can look like, showing off her physique in a bikini while demonstrating glute exercises in a bathroom. HILARIA BALDWIN FLAUNTS FIT FIGURE IN BIKINI AS FANS MARVEL AT MOM OF 7 Despite her fitness-focused lifestyle, Hilaria insisted she isn't living exclusively on lettuce. "It's not always the same," Hilaria said when asked what a typical day of meals looks like. "I think people think that I just eat salad all the time, which I’ve definitely done that in the past. But the other day — the baby of the family, we opened up pints of ice cream, two different pints of ice cream at 9 PM. So, sometimes it looks like that." WATCH: HILARIA BALDWIN SQUEEZES IN ‘BATHROOM WORKOUTS’ AS A MOM OF 7 She added, "Eat good things and then enjoy. Have the slice of pizza once in a while. Have the ice cream. I think it’s just a bit of a balance." When Fox News Digital asked if her husband, Alec Baldwin, ever joins her workouts, she laughed and said he’s not the most flexible person. "Can’t touch his toes. I literally married the most inflexible person I have ever met." 'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS After more than 15 years together, seven children and plenty of public scrutiny, Hilaria shared the relationship advice she said has helped keep her longtime relationship strong. articles.title: 'The Dog Stars' Review: Jacob Elordi fights for survival in Ridley Scott's dull post-apocalyptic western
articles.summary: Fox News Digital reviews 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars" starring Jacob Elordi, Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce and Allison Janney. Directed by Ridley Scott.
articles.body: Ridley Scott has directed some of Hollywood's most iconic movies, from "Alien" and "Blade Runner" to "Thelma & Louise" and "Gladiator." But over the past decade, his films have mostly ranged from OK to meh. Unfortunately, his latest falls in the latter category. "The Dog Stars," adapted from Peter Heller's 2012 novel, follows Hig (Jacob Elordi), a mechanic trying to navigate a post-apocalyptic America that had been ravaged by a deadly flu years earlier. He has taken shelter at an abandoned Colorado airport and is joined by Bangley (Josh Brolin), a brutish former Marine with great aim, and Hig's Belgian shepherd, Jasper. ‘MUTINY’ REVIEW: JASON STATHAM TAKES NO PRISONERS IN MINDLESS BUT AMUSING BRAWLER FLICK ON THE HIGH SEAS The routine is as follows: Hig flies into Denver in his little yellow plane to seek supplies, stops by his old house, triggering flashbacks of his late wife, occasionally makes deliveries to a rural community of Mennonite farmers, and sometimes joins Bangley in killing trespassers who may be infected with the virus before burning their bodies as a precaution. Hig thinks there is more civilization beyond the mountains, namely in Grand Junction. Bangley thinks it's a fool's errand and that leaving Eric would certainly lead to death. But Hig can't deny his own convictions, so he ultimately decides to seek life elsewhere. ‘THE END OF OAK STREET’ REVIEW: ANNE HATHAWAY, EWAN MCGREGOR FIGHT DINOSAURS IN SURPRISINGLY FUN MOVIE He'll come across some interesting characters on his journey, like the boorish rancher Jack and his daughter Cima (Guy Pearce and Margaret Qualley) and the eccentric Darlene (Allison Janney). There's also what's been dubbed the "Reapers," a group of tatted savages who will kill and destroy anything in their path. The cast does a fine job. Elordi, the Australian up-and-comer known for his breakout role in HBO's "Euphoria" and appearing more recently in "Wuthering Heights" and Netflix's "Frankenstein" (which earned him his first Oscar nomination), is flexing his leading man muscles. Both Brolin and Pearce earn a few laughs for their rough-around-the-edges performances. And Janney elevates any project she's in, regardless how zany her character is. 'TONY' REVIEW: ANTHONY BOURDAIN'S COMING-OF-AGE STORY UNFOLDS IN CHARMING DRAMEDY However, I never felt strongly invested as a viewer. Except for a few gun battles, "The Dog Stars" was fairly dull. Despite Elordi's best efforts, Hig is a run-of-the-mill dystopian protagonist, so there isn't much to work with (perhaps the source material is to blame). The guitar-forward score from Harry Gregson-Williams only furthers the film's sleepy western vibe. At least all the mountain scenery was pleasant to look at. ‘SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY’ REVIEW: TOM HOLLAND, ZENDAYA RETURN FOR ACTION-PACKED, EMOTIONAL SEQUEL CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The Verdict Ridley Scott's "The Dog Stars" is the latest installment in the prolific director's middling stretch of films that will likely leave the mind shortly after viewing. And when that happens, you question why the movie was made to begin with. ★★ — SKIP IT "The Dog Stars" is rated R for strong violence and language. Running time: 1 hour, 58 minutes. In theaters now. articles.title: Welcome to Night Vale cocreator Joseph Fink learned storytelling from Grim Fandango
articles.summary: Welcome to Night Vale and Alice Isn’t Dead creator Joseph Fink’s latest book The Nudge tells the story of a man trying to outrun a mysterious evil.
articles.body: Joseph Fink is the cocreator and cowriter of Welcome to Night Vale, arguably the most important fiction podcast ever. He’s also the creator of the noir podcast Unlicensed and Alice Isn’t Dead, which takes some of the conspiratorial cosmic horror of Night Vale and turns it into fodder for a more serious series about relationships, trauma, and the open road. There’s also a sequel series out now called Don’t Tell Alice that takes the story down an even darker path in which protagonist Keisha is the one with a secret. Joseph is also an accomplished author. In addition to co-writing the three Welcome to Night Vale novels, he’s also penned the Alice Isn’t Dead novel and The Halloween Moon. His latest work is The Nudge, which features some gorgeous illustrations from Jessica Hayworth, who also provides the art for Night Vale, hits shelves on September 1st. It’s a brief and unsettling novella about a man trying to outrun some mysterious evil. What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? Podcast Addict. It’s an Android-only podcast app made by one guy named Xavier, and it is so much better than any other podcast app that it’s the main reason I can never switch to an iPhone. I’m maybe the one guy in the entire country who chooses phones based on how they play podcasts. Which social media platform do you use the most? I use Bluesky, which I used to like because no one was there and so no one read my posts, which is really the ideal social media for me. Now there are more people there, and sometimes people read and respond to my posts, which is a drag. What game do you have the fondest memories of? My entire understanding of storytelling is probably shaped by Grim Fandango, a 1999 adventure game about a sad sack grim reaper navigating a film noir afterlife. There are lines and images from that game that will live in my head forever, even if a lot of them were parodies or references to classic films I wasn’t even aware existed when I first played that game. What creation are you most proud of? Our Audible show Unlicensed was one of those few projects that turned out exactly how I wanted it to in my head. A mystery series set in the least cool parts of Los Angeles, the parts where the actual people live. I didn’t want it to be “good for two writers who usually don’t write mysteries.” I just wanted us to write a damn good mystery, and I think we did. We got three seasons out of Audible, but then they mostly shut down their original shows department, and that was it. If I had my choice though, I’d happily spend the rest of my life writing Unlicensed. What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received? I recently watched a talk with Meshell Ndegeocello, and she described having to shush a fellow student in a guitar workshop who was noodling on his guitar while the teacher was trying to demonstrate something. Meshell said: “As a musician, it doesn’t matter how well you play if you can’t listen.” I don’t know if it’s the best advice I’ve ever received, but I think it’s damn good advice and applies to a lot of things outside of music. What’s the last piece of physical media you bought? I buy too many books, constantly. I like to hang out in bookstores, and I’ve never left one without buying at least a couple of books. I’m mostly not a physical media guy, I have no interest in owning records or DVDs, but I’ll build an addition to my house before I get rid of any books. What would the tagline for your biopic be? “It turns out watching a guy write audio fiction on his computer is boring, this movie was a mistake sorry, we’re sorry.” What’s the last GIF or meme you used? I don’t really use GIFs or memes. I’m very much a text guy, which is why I stick to text social media mostly, even though that doesn’t really help you sell books or stuff like that.

articles.title: Dolly Parton streams skyrocket after her death, making her the most streamed artist globally
articles.summary: Dolly Parton was many things: A country star, actor, philanthropist, entrepreneur, theme park enthusiast, Christian who centered acceptance in her personal theology and so much more.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Dolly Parton was many things: A country star, actor, philanthropist, entrepreneur, theme park enthusiast, Christian who centered acceptance in her personal theology and so much more. But for many, her death Tuesday has served as a reminder that at the heart of her legacy is her role as a songwriter. And around the world, people are streaming her songs en masse. According to evolving data released early Friday afternoon by the industry data and analytics company Luminate, audio and video streams of Parton’s discography skyrocketed 2,458% on the day of her death, compared to Monday — climbing from 1.2 million to 30.5 million in the U.S. And by Wednesday, that number rose to 46.3 million. Worldwide, her audio and video streams jumped 1,549%, from 2.5 million on Monday to 41.8 million Tuesday. And on Wednesday, her on-demand audio streams jumped to 79.7 million, making her the most streamed artist, globally, on that date. In the U.S., 10 songs led the charge: 1. “Jolene” grew from over 196.2K streams on Monday to 3.3 million Tuesday and 4 million Wednesday. 2. “9 to 5” jumped from 208.6K on Monday to 3.0 million on Tuesday and 3.6 million on Wednesday. 3. “Islands in the Stream,” her duet with the late Kenny Rogers, climbed from 165.9K on Monday to 2.1 million Tuesday and 2.9 million Wednesday. 4. “I Will Always Love You,” Parton’s performance of her own classic, a song that was later made famous by Whitney Houston’s rendition, rose from 64.9K streams on Monday to 2.0 million Tuesday and 2.8 million Wednesday. 5. “Here You Come Again” followed, moving from 48.7K streams Monday to 1.5 million Tuesday to 2.1 million Wednesday. 6. Then there was “Coat of Many Colors,” with 28.9K streams Monday to 1.3 million Tuesday and 1.9 million Wednesday. 7. “Why’d You Come In Here Lookin’ Like That?” climbed from 22.1K Monday to 827K Tuesday and 1.3 million Wednesday. 8. “There Was Jesus,” her 2019 duet with Christian singer Zach Williams, rose from 85.2K streams Monday to 635.1K Tuesday and 682.0K Wednesday. 9. “My Tennessee Mountain Home” increased from 5.8K Monday to 562.3K Tuesday and 1.1 million Wednesday. 10. “Tyrant,” Parton’s collaboration with Beyoncé from Bey’s Grammy winning 2024 album “Cowboy Carter,” jumped from 47.8K Monday to 559.2K Tuesday and 755.5K Wednesday. Sales for such Parton-related books as the memoir “Dolly Parton, Songteller” My Life in Lyrics” and a picture story based on her classic song “Coat of Many Colors” were also soaring. As of early Friday afternoon, three Parton books were in the top 5 on Amazon.com ’s bestseller list.
